About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Drama Years 11–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Drama Years 11–13 is still in development.
Once that is completed, Drama Years 11–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister
of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the
Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Drama Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from 1
January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Drama, Students are taught how to examine dramatic forms, conventions, and
  performance styles in relation to cultural and historical contexts, and how to apply
  this knowledge in the creation and presentation of dramatic work. They develop
  technical, collaborative, and interpretive skills, alongside critical reflection and
  informed appreciation of artistic works.

Students are taught the concepts, terminology, structures and frameworks used in
theatre-making, and how performance communicates meaning through acting,
directing, devising, scriptwriting, and design and technology.

Drama provides students with the knowledge and practices to create, perform,
analyse, and evaluate dramatic work. This disciplinary knowledge helps students
develop expertise in using drama techniques, theatrical conventions, and
performance processes, and in understanding how drama can reflect and respond to
human experiences.

As students progress through Year 11–13, they are taught to develop the ability to
interpret, analyse, evaluate, synthesise, and communicate dramatic ideas,
performances, texts, and theatrical practices. This enables them to communicate
ideas and perspectives effectively, collaborate responsibly, and respond thoughtfully
to cultural, social, and ethical contexts.

  Drama leads to pathways in drama and related disciplines, such as creative
  industries, law, communication, humanities, and education.

Responsible use of AI
Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative
processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues
relating to ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking,
source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students’ own analysis and decision-
making. Responsible AI use emphasises the importance of exercising independent
judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent
about AI use, considering diverse perspectives, and developing independent thinking.
In Performing Arts, where students use AI-assisted processes, they should critically
evaluate and direct their use of those tools, maintain ownership of creative decisions,
and ensure that creative works reflect their own artistic intent, experimentation, and
creative development.

Collaboration, collective responsibility, and safe practice
Drama is a collaborative discipline that relies on relationships, shared responsibility,
and care for people, processes, and stories. Students should be taught to contribute
and respond to ideas, collaborating respectfully with others, and sharing responsibility
for creative and production processes Establishing whanaungatanga requires building
positive working relationships through trust, respectful communication, and shared
commitment to collaborative processes. Concepts of care and respect, Manaakitanga
and kaitiakitanga, underpin directing practice through respectful leadership, clear
communication, and care for people and process. These principles affect how
dramatic work is created, rehearsed, refined, and performed and support strong
collaboration, constructive feedback, and ethical decision-making. They strengthen
practice and help create safe, productive rehearsal and performance environments.
